{{Short description|Parametrization used for loop integrals}}
{{for|the technique known as "Feynman's trick"|Leibniz integral rule#Evaluating definite integrals}}
'''Feynman parametrization''' is a technique for evaluating [[loop integral]]s which arise from [[Feynman diagram]]s with one or more loops. However, it is sometimes useful in integration in areas of [[pure mathematics]] as well. It was introduced by [[Julian Schwinger]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schwinger |first=Julian |date=1949-09-15 |title=Quantum Electrodynamics. III. The Electromagnetic Properties of the Electron---Radiative Corrections to Scattering |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.76.790 |journal=Physical Review |volume=76 |issue=6 |pages=790–817 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.76.790|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[Richard Feynman]]<ref name=":0" /> in 1949 to perform calculations in [[quantum electrodynamics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kim |first=U-Rae |last2=Cho |first2=Sungwoong |last3=Lee |first3=Jungil |date=2023 |title=The art of Schwinger and Feynman parametrizations |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s40042-023-00764-3 |journal=Journal of the Korean Physical Society |language=en |volume=82 |issue=11 |pages=1023–1039 |doi=10.1007/s40042-023-00764-3 |issn=0374-4884|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Peskin |first=Michael E. |url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/An_Introduction_To_Quantum_Field_Theory/HUpaDwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=peskin+schroeder&printsec=frontcover |title=An Introduction To Quantum Field Theory |date=2018-05-04 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-0-429-97210-2 |language=en}}</ref>{{Efn|Schwinger is credited as having published first. Feynman credits the method "suggested by some work of Schwinger’s involving Gaussian integrals".}}

[[Hung Cheng]] and [[Tai Tsun Wu|T.T. Wu]] proved in 1987<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cheng |first=H. |title=Expanding Protons: Scattering at High Energies |last2=Wu |first2=T.T. |date=1987 |publisher=MIT Press |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts}}</ref> that the sum in the [[Dirac delta function]] can be reduced to a subset of Feynman parameters. This result is known as '''Cheng–Wu theorem'''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abreu |first=Samuel |last2=Britto |first2=Ruth |last3=Duhr |first3=Claude |date=2022-11-04 |title=The SAGEX review on scattering amplitudes Chapter 3: Mathematical structures in Feynman integrals |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1751-8121/ac87de |journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical |volume=55 |issue=44 |pages=443004 |doi=10.1088/1751-8121/ac87de |issn=1751-8113|hdl=20.500.11820/6f37103c-45f7-471a-8097-0787968da159 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Formulas ==

=== Two denominators ===
Richard Feynman observed that<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Feynman |first=R. P. |date=1949-09-15 |title=Space-Time Approach to Quantum Electrodynamics |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.76.769 |journal=Physical Review |volume=76 |issue=6 |pages=769–789 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.76.769|bibcode=1949PhRv...76..769F }}</ref>

:<math>\frac{1}{AB}=\int^1_0 \frac{du}{\left[uA +(1-u)B\right]^2}</math>

which is valid for any complex numbers ''A'' and ''B'' as long as 0 is not contained in the line segment connecting ''A'' and ''B.'' The formula helps to evaluate integrals like:

:<math>\begin{align}
\int \frac{dp}{A(p)B(p)}
&= \int dp \int^1_0 \frac{du}{\left[uA(p)+(1-u)B(p)\right]^2} \\
&= \int^1_0 du \int \frac{dp}{\left[uA(p)+(1-u)B(p)\right]^2}.
\end{align}</math>

If ''A''(''p'') and ''B''(''p'') are linear functions of ''p'', then the last integral can be evaluated using substitution.

=== Multiple denominators ===
More generally, using the [[Dirac delta function]] <math>\delta</math>:<ref name="weinberg">{{cite book|last=Weinberg|first=Steven|title=The Quantum Theory of Fields, Volume I|date=2008|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|pages=497|isbn=978-0-521-67053-1}}</ref>

:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{A_1\cdots A_n}&= (n-1)! \int^1_0 du_1 \cdots \int^1_0 du_n \frac{\delta(1-\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{k})\;}{\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{k}A_{k}\right)^n} \\
&=(n-1)! \int^1_0 du_1 \int^{u_1}_0 du_2 \cdots \int^{u_{n-2}}_0 du_{n-1} \frac{1}{\left[A_1u_{n-1}+A_2(u_{n-2} - u_{n-1})+\dots+A_n(1 - u_1)\right]^n}.
\end{align}</math>

This formula is valid for any complex numbers ''A<sub>1</sub>'',...,''A<sub>n</sub>'' as long as 0 is not contained in their [[convex hull]].

Even more generally, provided that <math> \text{Re} ( \alpha_{j} ) > 0  </math> for all <math> 1 \leq j \leq n </math>:

:<math>\frac{1}{A_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots A_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}} = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{1}+\dots+\alpha_{n})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{1})\cdots\Gamma(\alpha_{n})}\int_{0}^{1}du_{1}\cdots\int_{0}^{1}du_{n}\frac{\delta(1-\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{k})\;u_{1}^{\alpha_{1}-1}\cdots u_{n}^{\alpha_{n}-1}}{\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}u_{k}A_{k}\right)^{\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}}}
 </math> 
where the [[Gamma function]] <math>\Gamma</math> was used.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.physic.ut.ee/~kkannike/english/science/physics/notes/feynman_param.pdf|title=Notes on Feynman Parametrization and the Dirac Delta Function|author=Kristjan Kannike|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070729015208/http://www.physic.ut.ee/~kkannike/english/science/physics/notes/feynman_param.pdf|archive-date=2007-07-29|access-date=2011-07-24}}</ref>

==Derivation==
:<math>\frac{1}{AB} = \frac{1}{A-B}\left(\frac{1}{B}-\frac{1}{A}\right)=\frac{1}{A-B}\int_B^A \frac{dz}{z^2}.</math>
By using the substitution <math>u=(z-B)/(A-B)</math>, we have <math>du = dz/(A-B)</math>, and <math>z = uA + (1-u)B</math>, from which we get the desired result
:<math>\frac{1}{AB} = \int_0^1 \frac{du}{\left[uA + (1-u)B\right]^2}.</math>

In more general cases, derivations can be done very efficiently using the [[Schwinger parametrization]]. For example, in order to derive the Feynman parametrized form of <math> \frac{1}{A_1...A_n} </math>, we first reexpress all the factors in the denominator in their Schwinger parametrized form:

:<math>\frac{1}{A_i}= \int^\infty_0 ds_i \, e^{-s_i A_i} \ \ \text{for } i =1,\ldots,n </math>
and rewrite,

:<math>
\frac{1}{A_1\cdots A_n}=\int_0^\infty ds_1\cdots \int_0^\infty ds_n \exp\left(-\left(s_1A_1+\cdots+s_nA_n\right)\right).
</math>

Then we perform the following change of integration variables,
:<math> 
\alpha  =  s_1+...+s_n,
</math>
:<math> 
\alpha_{i} = \frac{s_{i}}{s_1+\cdots+s_n}; \ i=1,\ldots,n-1,
</math>
to obtain,
:<math>
\frac{1}{A_1\cdots A_n} = \int_{0}^{1}d\alpha_1\cdots d\alpha_{n-1} \int_{0}^{\infty}d\alpha\ \alpha^{n-1}\exp\left(-\alpha\left\{ \alpha_1A_1+\cdots+\alpha_{n-1}A_{n-1}+ \left(1-\alpha_{1}-\cdots-\alpha_{n-1}\right)A_{n}\right\} \right).
</math>
where <math display="inline">\int_{0}^{1}d\alpha_1\cdots d\alpha_{n-1} </math> denotes integration over the region  <math> 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq 1</math> with <math display="inline"> \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \alpha_i \leq 1 </math>.

The next step is to perform the <math>\alpha </math> integration.

:<math>
\int_{0}^{\infty}d\alpha\ \alpha^{n-1}\exp(-\alpha x)= \frac{\partial^{n-1}}{\partial(-x)^{n-1}}\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}d\alpha\exp(-\alpha x)\right)=\frac{\left(n-1\right)!}{x^{n}}.
</math>  
where we have defined <math> x= \alpha_1A_1+\cdots+\alpha_{n-1}A_{n-1}+ \left(1-\alpha_{1}-\cdots-\alpha_{n-1}\right)A_{n}.</math>

Substituting this result, we get to the penultimate form,
:<math> 
\frac{1}{A_1\cdots A_n}=\left(n-1\right)!\int_{0}^{1}d\alpha_1\cdots d\alpha_{n-1}\frac{1}{[\alpha_1A_1+\cdots+\alpha_{n-1}A_{n-1}+ \left(1-\alpha_{1}-\cdots-\alpha_{n-1}\right)A_{n}]^n} ,
</math>
and, after introducing an extra integral, we arrive at the final form of the Feynman parametrization, namely,
:<math> 
\frac{1}{A_1\cdots A_n}=\left(n-1\right)!\int_{0}^{1}d\alpha_1\cdots\int_{0}^{1}d\alpha_{n}\frac{\delta\left(1-\alpha_1-\cdots-\alpha_n\right)}{[\alpha_1A_1+\cdots+\alpha_{n}A_{n}]^n} .
</math>

Similarly, in order to derive the Feynman parametrization form of the most general case,<math display="inline"> \frac{1}{A_1^{\alpha_1}...A_n^{\alpha_n}} </math> one could begin with the suitable different Schwinger parametrization form of factors in the denominator, namely,
 
:<math> 
\frac{1}{A_1^{\alpha_1}} = \frac{1}{\left(\alpha_1-1\right)!}\int^\infty_0 ds_1 \,s_1^{\alpha_1-1} e^{-s_1 A_1} =  \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha_1)}\frac{\partial^{\alpha_1-1}}{\partial(-A_1)^{\alpha_1-1}}\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}ds_1 e^{-s_1 A_1}\right)
</math>
and then proceed exactly along the lines of previous case.

==Alternative form==
An alternative form of the parametrization that is sometimes useful is
:<math>\frac{1}{AB} = \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{d\lambda}{\left[\lambda A + B\right]^2}.</math>

This form can be derived using the change of variables <math>\lambda = u / ( 1 - u ) </math>.
We can use the [[product rule]] to show that <math> d\lambda = du/(1-u)^{2} </math>, then
:<math>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{AB} & = \int^1_0 \frac{du}{\left[uA +(1-u)B\right]^2} \\
& = \int^1_0 \frac{du}{(1-u)^{2}} \frac{1}{\left[\frac{u}{1-u} A + B \right]^2} \\
& = \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{d\lambda}{\left[\lambda A + B\right]^2} \\
\end{align}</math>

More generally we have
:<math>\frac{1}{A^{m}B^{n}} = \frac{\Gamma( m+n)}{\Gamma(m)\Gamma(n)}\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{\lambda^{m-1}d\lambda}{\left[\lambda A + B\right]^{n+m}},</math>
where <math> \Gamma </math> is the [[gamma function]].

This form can be useful when combining a linear denominator <math> A </math> with a quadratic denominator <math> B </math>, such as in [[heavy quark effective theory]] (HQET).

==Symmetric form==
A symmetric form of the parametrization is occasionally used, where the integral is instead performed on the interval <math>[-1,1] </math>, leading to:

:<math>\frac{1}{AB} = 2\int_{-1}^1 \frac{du}{\left[(1+u)A + (1-u)B\right]^2}.</math>
